questions.stem: The 'Fundamental Duties' were not present in the original Constitution of India. Which Constitutional Amendment Act added them in 1976?

options.option_text: 42nd Amendment Act
44th Amendment Act
73rd Amendment Act
86th Amendment Act

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The original Constitution (1950) only contained Fundamental Rights, not duties. During the Emergency (1975-77), the Swaran Singh Committee recommended incorporating Fundamental Duties. Based on this, the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1976 added a new Part IV-A and a single new Article 51A, listing 10 Fundamental Duties for citizens.
DECOY BUSTING: The 44th Amendment (1978) undid many of the 42nd Amendment's excesses and removed the Right to Property. The 73rd added Panchayats. The 86th (2002) added Education as a fundamental right.
EXAM INSIGHT: The concept of Fundamental Duties was borrowed from the Constitution of the erstwhile Soviet Union (USSR). Crucially, the 86th Amendment (2002) added an 11th duty (to provide education to children aged 6-14).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Like the Directive Principles of State Policy, the Fundamental Duties in the Indian Constitution are:

options.option_text: Non-justiciable
Justiciable
Applicable only to government officials
Applicable to both citizens and foreigners

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable in nature. This means you cannot be directly taken to court and punished SOLELY for violating a fundamental duty (e.g., if you fail to "strive towards excellence", the police cannot arrest you). However, Parliament is free to enforce them by passing specific laws (e.g., the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act enforces the duty to respect the National Flag).
DECOY BUSTING: Fundamental Rights are Justiciable (you can go to court if they are violated). Fundamental Duties apply ONLY to Indian citizens, not foreigners.
EXAM INSIGHT: In legal interpretations, the Supreme Court often uses Fundamental Duties to determine the constitutional validity of a law. If a law seeks to enforce a fundamental duty, the court may consider it "reasonable" and uphold it.

questions.stem: Fundamental Duties of Indian citizens are enumerated in which Part and Article of the Constitution?

options.option_text: Part III, Articles 12–35 — the Fundamental Rights chapter
Part IV-A, Article 51A — inserted by the 42nd Amendment
Part IV, Articles 36–51 — the Directive Principles chapter
Part IVB, Article 51B — added alongside the 43rd Amendment

questions.explanation: Fundamental Duties are contained in Part IV-A (a new Part inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976) under the single Article 51A. They are neither in Part III (Fundamental Rights) nor Part IV (DPSPs). Option D is a fabricated provision — no Part IVB or Article 51B exists in the Constitution.

questions.stem: The 11th Fundamental Duty — requiring a parent or guardian to provide educational opportunities to their child aged 6–14 years — was added by which Constitutional Amendment?

options.option_text: 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 — which added the original ten duties
44th Amendment Act, 1978 — Janata government's post-Emergency reforms
86th Amendment Act, 2002 — which also inserted Article 21A on RTE
91st Amendment Act, 2003 — related to anti-defection strengthening

questions.explanation: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 simultaneously inserted Article 21A (Right to Education as a Fundamental Right), added the 11th Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(k), and amended Article 45 of DPSPs to focus on early childhood care. The 44th Amendment (1978) addressed rights after the Emergency but did not touch Fundamental Duties.

questions.stem: How many Fundamental Duties were originally incorporated by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, and what is the current total under Article 51A?

options.option_text: 8 original duties; the current total stands at 9 in Article 51A
10 original duties; the current total stands at 11 in Article 51A
9 original duties; the current total stands at 12 in Article 51A
12 original duties; the current total stands at 14 in Article 51A

questions.explanation: The 42nd Amendment (1976), based on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendations, inserted 10 Fundamental Duties under clauses (a) to (j) of Article 51A. The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 added one more — clause (k) — making the current total 11. No subsequent amendment has altered this count. Options A and C contain fabricated figures that candidates must not confuse.

questions.stem: Which clause of Article 51A most directly captures the idea of 'composite nationalism' by acknowledging India's multi-religious and multi-cultural character?

options.option_text: Clause (b) — cherish noble ideals that inspired the national freedom struggle
Clause (e) — promote harmony and spirit of common brotherhood among all citizens
Clause (f) — value and preserve the rich heritage of India's composite culture
Clause (c) — uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India

questions.explanation: Clause (f) explicitly uses the phrase 'composite culture', which in constitutional jurisprudence denotes India's syncretic tradition blending diverse religions, languages and ethnicities. Clause (e) is the most tempting distractor — it promotes harmony and brotherhood — but it does not use the term 'composite culture' or specifically recognise India's pluralist cultural heritage.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched — Fundamental Duty clause and its content under Article 51A?

options.option_text: Clause (a) — abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and symbols
Clause (d) — defend the country and render national service when called upon
Clause (i) — cherish and follow noble ideals of the independence movement
Clause (g) — protect and improve natural environment including forests and wildlife

questions.explanation: Clause (i) of Article 51A reads: 'to safeguard public property and to abjure violence' — it has nothing to do with the independence movement. The duty to cherish noble ideals of the national freedom struggle belongs to Clause (b). This is a classic PYQ trap: candidates who memorise the spirit rather than the exact clause numbering routinely swap (b) and (i). Options A, B and D are correctly matched.

questions.stem: Fundamental Duties under Part IV-A of the Indian Constitution are binding upon which of the following categories of persons?

options.option_text: Citizens of India only; foreigners residing in India are excluded
Both Indian citizens and all foreign nationals residing in India
Only central government employees and elected public representatives
Citizens and registered Overseas Citizens of India (OCI) cardholders

questions.explanation: Article 51A opens with 'It shall be the duty of every citizen of India' — making Fundamental Duties applicable exclusively to citizens. Foreign nationals and aliens are not covered, even if resident in India. OCI cardholders are also excluded as they do not hold citizenship under Articles 5–11. This contrasts with certain Fundamental Rights (Articles 14, 21) that extend to 'all persons'. Option B is a common conflation error.

questions.stem: Regarding the legal enforceability of Fundamental Duties, which of the following statements is constitutionally most accurate?

options.option_text: Parliament may enact penal laws to enforce Fundamental Duties on citizens
Citizens can file writs in High Courts to enforce duties against the State
All existing criminal statutes automatically enforce each Fundamental Duty
High Courts can issue mandamus compelling citizens to perform their duties

questions.explanation: Though Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable (courts cannot directly enforce them), Parliament can legislate to make their violation a punishable offence — for example, the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 gives penal teeth to Clause (a). Option B is wrong: writs enforce rights against the State, not duties upon citizens. Option D is wrong: mandamus issues against public authorities, not private citizens. Option C is wrong: no blanket automatic enforcement exists.
